title: Ha'azinu: the eagle over its nest (Deuteronomy 32:11)
hookLine: God cares like an eagle that stirs its nest and spreads its wings
tomorrow: V'Zot HaBerachah: end with a blessing (Deuteronomy 33:1)

lines: A WARM NEST, A LONG DROP.
PUSH, BUT DON'T LET THEM FALL.
cards: Sooner or later, a young bird has to leave the nest. The nest is warm, food arrives on schedule, and the edge looks very far down.
The parent has a problem: how do you push someone toward the thing that scares them without letting them fall? Parents of teenagers meet the same problem. So do teachers and coaches.
Ha'azinu answers it with a picture.

teach.b: "As an eagle that stirreth up her nest, Hovereth over her young, Spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, Beareth them on her pinions." That's how, the song says, God cared for the people in the wilderness.
Four movements. Stir the nest: wake them, get them ready. Hover: stay close, without pressing down.
Spread the wings: make a place for them to land. Bear them up: carry them while they can't yet fly. Rashi reads the details tenderly.
The eagle, he says, doesn't swoop straight down onto its young.

teach.h: NO FULL WEIGHT ON THE NEST.
teach.b: It flutters over the nest to wake them gently, and hovers without putting its full weight on them.

teach.h: ON THE WINGS, NOT IN THE CLAWS.
teach.b: And when it carries them, it carries them on its wings, not in its claws. Other birds, Rashi says, carry their young in their feet, because they fear a bigger bird above.
The eagle fears only an arrow shot from below, so it puts its own body between the arrow and its young.

teach.h: I BORE YOU ON EAGLES' WINGS.
teach.b: The same picture appears at Sinai, in Exodus, where God says to the people: "how I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself."
Protection here isn't keeping someone in the nest forever. It's stirring them to grow, and staying underneath while they learn to fly.

how: The image of God bearing Israel on eagles' wings, from Exodus 19 and Ha'azinu, is a familiar one in Jewish teaching and song, often used to describe care that protects without smothering.

o: bless: the words Moses gives the tribes
give ear: the opening word of Moses' song
go up: Moses climbing the mountain

games.q: the eagle's four movements — tap the pairs.
p: wakes the young, gets them ready

s: Rashi says the eagle carries its young in its claws
on its wings, with its body between them and the arrow.
the eagles' wings picture also appears at Sinai

games.q: you're the eagle in Rashi's reading, and the only danger is a hunter's arrow from below. how do you carry your young?
o: on your wings, your body between them and the arrow.
you leave them in the nest.
games.why: Rashi: better the arrow strike me than my young. protection that puts itself underneath.

practice: Think of someone you care for who's trying something new, and ask where you are on the eagle's list: stirring, hovering, spreading your wings, carrying, or pressing down with your full weight.
Picture loosening your grip, staying close and underneath, letting them try. And if you're the one in the nest right now, picture someone hovering nearby, close enough to catch you if you fall.

wordCard.voice: Ha'azinu. Give ear. And the eagle in the song, stirring the nest and spreading its wings beneath its young.

orig.note: Hebrew: eagle, though some scholars think the bird meant is the griffon vulture.

carryVoice: Your line: spread the wings. On the wings, not in the claws. Day five hundred thirty-one.
